findings.title: All 24 numbers on the original report reproduce, and 21 needed a fix or a caveat
findings.summary: Recomputing each card from the report's own tables matches every number it showed. Following the model's relationships explains the odd ones: the Mobility page's date slicer sat on the cycling table, whose links to walking speed and step length were inactive, so those cards showed all-time averages. Walking speed read 2.61 mph; for the page's own dates (May 1, 2024 to Aug 1, 2024) it was 2.52. The stand card read 127 "hours", which is 2.1 hours of standing.
findings.metric: Each card was recomputed in pandas from the aggregation, filters and relationships stored in the report layout and data model.
findings.caveat: The displayed values were transcribed from the March 2025 report screenshots; the tolerance is the precision each card showed.

findings.title: The original report counted walking distance about twice
findings.summary: Steps were filtered to the watch, but distance kept every device, so a walk logged by both the watch and the phone counted twice. At a median step length of 26.5 inches, 1,000 steps cover about 0.42 miles. The original table recorded 0.84; the rebuild, which keeps one device per hour, records 0.44.
findings.metric: Median of daily miles ÷ steps × 1,000 on days with at least 1,000 steps, against step length × 1,000 ÷ 63,360.
findings.caveat: Step length comes from the phone's walking metrics, which start in late 2020; the median is applied to every year.

findings.title: Keeping one device per hour removes about 27% of raw steps
findings.summary: Adding up every step record in the export gives 9,282 steps a day. Keeping one device per hour (the watch when it was worn, the phone otherwise) gives 6,819. Unlike the original report, phone-only hours still count, so days without the watch are no longer blank.
findings.metric: Daily sums with and without the de-duplication step, over every day in the export.
findings.caveat: Health's own merge works on finer intervals than an hour, so daily totals can differ slightly from the Health app.

findings.title: More exercise went with a lower resting heart rate (r = −0.71)
findings.summary: Across 72 months with at least 15 days of data, months with more exercise had a lower resting heart rate and higher heart rate variability (r = 0.83). Through 2020 the average was 17 exercise minutes a day and a resting heart rate of 72 bpm; from 2023 it was 57 minutes and 63 bpm, with 1,320 workouts logged since the start of 2023.
findings.metric: Pearson correlation of monthly means. The drop shows on the same watch too: 72.5 bpm in 2019 against 60.9 bpm in January to August 2023.
findings.caveat: A correlation across months, not proof that one caused the other. Sleep, stress and season also move resting heart rate.

findings.title: Three daily rules in the original query were wrong for their metric
findings.summary: Running power was summed per day, giving totals such as 98,328 W. Headphone exposure kept each day's quietest reading, with nine tiny values hard-coded out. Environmental sound was averaged arithmetically, which understates decibels: on the same 434 days the energy average is 7.5 dB higher.
findings.metric: Each table's daily rule was read from its Power Query step (List.Sum, List.Min, List.Average) and compared with the rebuild's rule.
findings.caveat: Each rebuilt rule is documented in metrics.py and covered by a test on a hand-written fixture.
